findings.title: Missing upper-bound clamp on LLM-supplied timeout_seconds; code_exec has the clamp, code_check does not
findings.rationale: code_check shares its `code: ArgCheckArgs.timeout_seconds: Option<u64>` shape with code_exec, where the value is explicitly clamped via `clamp_foreground_timeout` (FOREGROUND_MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS = 170) inside `AlephTool::call`. code_check bypasses `call_unclamped` — yet still passes `args.timeout_seconds.unwrap_or(120)` straight into `Duration::from_secs(timeout_secs)` and a `SandboxCommand::timeout`. An LLM caller (or a stuck tool loop) passing `u64::MAX` reserves a 2.6e11-second sandbox lease that pegs a worker for years. The default of 120s is generous for cold `cargo check`; without the clamp the 180s per-tool budget wrapper does NOT fire (it tracks wall-clock from the call site, not the sandbox lease), so a runaway checker is the caller's problem, not the budget's. Pattern matches the GOOD code_exec.rs:793 site verbatim.

findings.context: pub async fn call() — session-raw fact retrieval branch
findings.title: max_results is documented as LLM-supplied and unclamped; saturating_mul(2) hides the DoS
findings.after:
const MAX_RESULTS: usize = 50; // matches recall_context
                let fetch_limit = args
                    .max_results
                    .clamp(1, MAX_RESULTS)
                    .saturating_mul(2);
                let raws = self
                    .database
                    .get_raw_by_path_prefix(&path_prefix, agent_id, fetch_limit)
                    .await
findings.rationale: The inline comment admits the design defect: the only defence against `usize::MAX` is `saturating_mul` (prevents the overflow-panic, not the allocation). `get_raw_by_path_prefix(..., usize::MAX)` will hand back the full raw-chunk table for the session (compact-then-paginated batches), each row then copied into a `FactResult` and accumulated into a `Vec`. Sister tool `recall_context` (`recall_context.rs:55-56`) explicitly caps at 3 by default and `recall_events` clamps to `[1, 20]`; sister `ctx_search` / `session_search` / `channel_directory` all `.clamp(1, MAX_LIMIT)`. `memory_search` is the only one of the retrieval tools that trusts the cap, and it is the largest — the same surface a model reach-for first. Other call sites that forward `args.max_results` verbatim: lines 559, 598, 656, 661, 676 — every one of them feeds a vector-store `retrieve` call that is already O(n*k).

findings.title: Background-mode timeout has no upper bound; foreground has one and is named the same
findings.rationale: Foreground enforces a 170s cap (FOREGROUND_MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS) precisely so the harness budget wrapper stays the enforcer. Background escapes that wrapper (the spawn call returns a process_id immediately) and is treated as trust-the-caller. With `background: true` and `timeout_seconds: u64::MAX` the daemon registers a job that the registry will never reap until it exits on its own — the kill path requires the same session to come back and call `process_action: "kill"`, and a stuck LLM that issued the bad call cannot. A 4h ceiling matches the 1h default but bounds the worst case. process_registry already enforces `MAX_RUNNING_PER_SESSION = 8` / `MAX_RUNNING_GLOBAL = 32`, but those bound COUNT, not DURATION per job.

findings.title: Silent discard `let _ = id_tx.send(id)` swallows registration-then-task-loss races
findings.rationale: `register_running` succeeded and the foreground returned `{"status":"running", "process_id": id, ...}` to the model. If the spawned task had already failed to receive the oneshot (panic before .await, or task-local re-entry crash inside the gated body), the model is told the job is running while the registry now holds an orphan whose live tail is wired to a dead task. The `_ =` is currently safe in practice (the gate awaits the oneshot inside the spawned task, so it cannot exit before receiving) but the pattern is one refactor away from a real silent orphan, and AGENTS.md flags silent-discards of fallible calls.

findings.title: call_unclamped has no audit trail; only the comment warns about it
findings.rationale: `call_unclamped` is a footgun-by-design — same sandbox call as `call`, just with the safety clamp skipped. The doc is the only thing stopping a future refactor from wiring it from a UI panel, a CLI retry, or a recovery loop and bypassing the 170s budget. Today the only caller is `BashExecTool::spawn_background` (line 311), so adding a structured log here would catch drift for free. No code change needed; mark the surface so audit can grep it.
